# How to Turn a Selfie Into a Polaroid-Style Portrait With a Gemini Prompt

> **In short:** Gemini can generate images from a written prompt. By describing your subject, outfit, lighting, and frame in a four-part structure, you can get a Polaroid-style portrait. Results vary — you'll likely need two or three tries to get one that feels right.

You have a selfie you like — the angle works, the light was kind, you actually felt like yourself. Now you want it to look like it was shot on a Polaroid camera in 1997: soft flash, faded colors, a chunky white border, maybe a scribbled caption. You can describe that look in words, and Google's Gemini can turn those words into an image. The trick is giving Gemini enough structure that it has something specific to work with — not just "make me a polaroid."

## Before you start
- A Google account you can sign in with.
- Access to Gemini — either the website (gemini.google.com) or the Gemini mobile app. Image creation may sit behind a paid Google AI plan on some accounts, so check your plan if the image option is missing.
- One clear, well-lit selfie saved on your device (phone or computer). Front-facing, no sunglasses, plain background works best.
- About five minutes total, plus a little patience — getting the look you want usually takes two or three rounds.

## Step 1 — Open Gemini and start a fresh chat
Open **gemini.google.com** in a browser, or launch the **Gemini app** on your phone. Sign in with the same Google account you use for Gmail or YouTube if asked. Once you're in, look for the **"New chat"** button — usually a plus icon, a pencil, or the words "New chat" near the top of the chat list. Tap or click it.

You should see a clean, empty chat box waiting for your first message. Starting fresh matters: image generation works best when the prompt is the only instruction Gemini has to focus on, with no leftover instructions from a previous conversation.

💬 Example: don't type anything yet — just confirm the chat is empty.

If it looks different: on older versions or some Android setups, the entry point is **"Gemini" inside the Google app** (the "G" logo) rather than a separate Gemini app. Either way, you should land on a chat screen with a text box at the bottom.

**You'll know it worked when** you see an empty message field and no previous conversation threads.

## Step 2 — Attach your selfie as a visual reference
In the empty chat box, look for an **attachment icon** — usually a paperclip, a plus sign, or an image icon near the text field. Tap it and pick **"Upload from device"** (or a similar option). Choose the selfie you prepared. Wait for the image to finish uploading — you'll see a small thumbnail of your photo appear in the message box.

Attaching a reference photo gives Gemini something to anchor the look to: your general face shape, hair, skin tone, and what you were wearing. Without a photo, Gemini is guessing what you look like from words alone, and the result rarely feels like you.

💬 Example: don't type a prompt yet — just attach the selfie and watch the thumbnail appear.

If it looks different: on some Gemini surfaces, the attachment icon is hidden inside a **"+"** or **"Tools"** menu next to the text box. If you can't find an upload button at all, your current Gemini surface may not support image inputs — in that case, skip this step and rely on a very detailed text description in Step 3.

**You'll know it worked when** a small image preview of your selfie is sitting in the chat box, ready to be sent with a prompt.

## Step 3 — Write the polaroid prompt using the four-part structure
Click into the text box and type your prompt using this structure: **(1) subject, (2) outfit, (3) lighting, (4) frame.** Think of these four slots as a recipe — each one nudges the image in a specific direction. Skip one and the result drifts toward generic.

Here's the template, with each slot filled in as an example:

💬 Example: *"Polaroid photo of a young woman with shoulder-length wavy hair and a small nose ring, soft half-smile. She is wearing a cream knit sweater and silver hoop earrings. Direct on-camera flash against a dark indoor background, slight red-eye, no fill light. White Polaroid 600 border with a handwritten caption 'spring break '98' in blue pen across the bottom. Soft focus, slightly overexposed, faded 90s film colors, square 1:1."*

You can swap the gender, hair, outfit, lighting, or caption — just keep all four slots filled. The **frame slot is the most important for the Polaroid look**: without "Polaroid," "white border," "handwritten caption," and "faded film colors," Gemini produces a normal photo, not a vintage one. Press **Enter** (or the send arrow) to send.

If it looks different: on some Gemini surfaces, image generation lives behind a separate **"Create image"** or **"Image"** toggle instead of happening automatically. If your prompt returns only text and no image, look in the input area for that option and try again with it selected.

**You'll know it worked when** Gemini generates an image (not just text) within a few seconds. The image should have a white border, look slightly washed-out, and roughly match the four things you described.

## Step 4 — Review the result and decide what to fix
Look at the generated image and compare it to your selfie. Don't judge it yet — just notice three things: **(a) Does it look like you, even vaguely?** **(b) Does it actually look like a Polaroid?** **(c) Is the outfit, lighting, or pose way off?**

Most first attempts miss on at least one of these. That's normal. Gemini generates one strong guess per prompt — it doesn't "see" your feedback the way a designer would. The way to steer it is to **rewrite your prompt** with a small change and send it again as a fresh message.

If the face is wrong but the style is right: add more face details (eye color, jaw shape, hairline, distinguishing features like glasses or freckles). If the style is wrong but the face is close: keep the face description and rewrite the **lighting** and **frame** slots with stronger Polaroid cues — try "direct on-camera flash," "warm color cast," "thick uneven white border."

💬 Example: *"The face looks a bit too round — change to: 'oval face, high cheekbones, straight nose, dark brown eyebrows.' Also add: 'visible film grain, slightly crooked white border like a real Polaroid.'"*

**You'll know it worked when** the next image lands closer to what you imagined. Two or three rounds is usually enough.

## Step 5 — Save the image to your device
Hover over or long-press the generated image. Look for a **download button** (usually a downward arrow icon), or a **"Save"** or **"Download"** option in a small menu that appears. The image saves to your phone's Photos or Gallery folder, or your computer's Downloads folder.

💬 Example: don't type anything — just click download and check your Photos or Downloads folder.

If it looks different: on the mobile app, you may need to tap the image first to open it full-screen, then look for a **share icon** (a square with an arrow pointing up) and pick **"Save image."** If you don't see any download option, a screenshot cropped to the image works in a pinch.

**You'll know it worked when** the Polaroid portrait shows up in your phone's gallery or computer's Downloads, ready to send.

## Common mistakes
- **Skipping the frame details.** A prompt that says "make this a polaroid" without mentioning "white border," "handwritten caption," or "faded film colors" usually produces a normal photo with a filter. The frame slot is what sells the look — be specific.
- **Describing yourself in a way Gemini can't anchor to.** Saying "make it look like me" without attaching a selfie or describing concrete features (hair color, face shape, glasses, freckles) gives Gemini nothing to work with. Either upload a reference photo or write at least three concrete face details.
- **Re-sending the exact same prompt.** Image generation is one-shot per prompt — sending the same prompt twice gives you two slightly different guesses, but doesn't "fix" the first one. Change one slot (usually lighting or face details) each round.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A Polaroid-style portrait makes a great profile photo for social media, a chat app, or a group-chat sticker — it stands out from the usual filtered selfies without needing a photo editor.
- **For your business or work:** If you run a small brand, newsletter, or side project, a Polaroid-style portrait of yourself feels personal and warm in a way a stock headshot doesn't. You can make a set of three or four in different "outfits" by just changing one slot in the prompt.
- **If you're just getting started:** The easiest first move is to fill in the template with the most ordinary, true description of yourself you can. Don't try to make it artistic on the first try — get the structure working, then get creative.

## Try it now
Open Gemini and paste this exact prompt, then swap the bracketed parts for your own details:

*"Polaroid photo of [describe yourself in two sentences — face, hair, expression]. Wearing [one clothing item]. Direct flash, dark background. White Polaroid border with caption 'first try' in blue pen. Faded 90s film colors, soft focus, square."*
